lesson.title: Multiplying Same-Base Powers: Why You Add the Exponents
lesson.summary: When two powers share the same base, you can multiply them by keeping the base and adding the exponents, a shortcut that comes directly from what a power actually counts.
lesson.body:
A power like x^4 is just a compact way of writing repeated multiplication: x times x times x times x, four factors of x in a row. Once you remember that an exponent is really a count of how many times the base appears as a factor, the product rule for exponents stops being a rule to memorize and becomes something you can reconstruct on the spot. If x^3 means 3 factors of x, and x^4 means 4 factors of x, then multiplying x^3 by x^4 just lines up all those factors together: 3 factors followed by 4 more factors, which is 7 factors of x in total, or x^7.

That reasoning gives the general product rule: for the same base a, a^m times a^n equals a^(m+n). The key restriction is that the bases have to match. You can combine x^3 times x^4 because both powers use x as the base, but you cannot combine x^3 times y^4 into a single power, because x and y are different quantities and their factors cannot be merged into one count.

Try the numeric check with 2^3 times 2^4. Expanding directly, 2^3 = 8 and 2^4 = 16, so 2^3 times 2^4 = 8 times 16 = 128. Using the product rule instead, 2^3 times 2^4 = 2^(3+4) = 2^7. Since 2^7 = 128, the two methods agree exactly, which confirms the rule is doing the same job as direct multiplication, just faster.

The rule extends naturally to expressions with coefficients out front, as long as you treat the coefficients and the variable powers as separate jobs. To simplify 3x^2 times 5x^5, first multiply the coefficients: 3 times 5 = 15. Then apply the product rule to the variable parts: x^2 times x^5 = x^(2+5) = x^7. Putting the pieces back together gives 3x^2 times 5x^5 = 15x^7. You can sanity-check the exponent by counting factors again: x^2 contributes 2 factors of x and x^5 contributes 5 more, for 7 factors total, matching x^7.

This rule leans directly on the idea of a power that you built in earlier lessons, where a^n was defined as repeated multiplication of a by itself n times. Everything here is just bookkeeping for that definition: instead of writing out every factor and recounting them by hand, you add the exponents because addition is exactly what counting combined groups of factors amounts to. Keep this base-matching requirement in mind, because it is the single most common mistake with this rule, applying it to powers that do not actually share a base.

The rule also handles a base with no visible exponent, since a variable written alone, like x, is understood to carry an exponent of 1. So x times x^6 is really x^1 times x^6, which combines to x^(1+6) = x^7. It is easy to forget that invisible 1 and mistakenly treat x as having no exponent at all, which would break the counting logic the rule depends on. It helps to briefly connect this rule to the zero exponent idea from the previous lesson: if you multiply x^5 by x^0, the product rule gives x^(5+0) = x^5, and since x^0 = 1, this is just x^5 times 1, which is x^5, so the two rules agree with each other exactly as they should. One more worked example ties the pieces together with three factors instead of two. Simplify 2x^3 times 3x^2 times x^4. Multiply the coefficients first: 2 times 3 times 1 (the invisible coefficient on x^4) = 6. Then add the exponents on the matching base: 3 + 2 + 4 = 9. The product rule extends naturally to more than two powers because the same factor-counting argument applies no matter how many groups of factors you are lining up end to end. So 2x^3 times 3x^2 times x^4 simplifies to 6x^9.
